Read About Ushuaia

A prison town at the bottom of the map that became the world's front door to Antarctica — and never quite stopped being both at once.

The bay that penetrates to the west

Ushuaia takes its name from the Yaghan language, spoken by the canoe-based people who lived along the Beagle Channel for some six thousand years before anyone else arrived. Ush waia means roughly "the bay that penetrates to the west," a plain description of the deep, sheltered harbor the city is built around. The Yaghan had no reason to name the place anything grander — it was simply where the water cut furthest into the land, a good spot for canoes.

The "end of the world" branding that now covers every sign, sticker and coffee cup downtown is a much later invention, but it isn't exactly wrong. Ushuaia is the southernmost city of its size on the planet, sitting on the Argentine side of an island cut in half by treaty with Chile, at the very tip of a continent that most maps run out of room to finish drawing. The Yaghan named a bay. Everyone since has been naming an idea.

Fire seen from the water

Tierra del Fuego — Land of Fire — was named in 1520, not by anyone who lived there but by Ferdinand Magellan, sailing through the strait that now carries his name and spotting the signal fires the Yaghan and Selk'nam people kept burning along the coast. Magellan himself apparently favored "Land of Smoke," reasoning that you light a fire to be seen, not to be admired, but the Spanish crown preferred the more dramatic version and Fire won out. Three centuries later, Charles Darwin sailed the same channel aboard the Beagle and wrote with real unease about the "wild and broken" coastline and the people living on it in a climate he could barely tolerate in a coat. The Beagle Channel he helped chart is the same water every catamaran in Ushuaia's harbor still runs today.

The Yaghan named a bay. Everyone since has been naming an idea.

A prison with a country attached

Ushuaia as an Argentine city dates to October 1884, when Commodore Augusto Lasserre — the man half the streets downtown are now named after — landed with a small government expedition to plant a flag in territory Chile also claimed. A flag alone doesn't hold ground, so Buenos Aires did what remote 19th-century governments often did with land they needed populated: it sent prisoners. The first inmates arrived in 1896, and construction began in 1902 on the stone cell blocks that still stand today as the Museo Marítimo y del Presidio de Ushuaia. For the next four and a half decades, convict labor built the roads, laid the bricks and cut the timber that turned a Yaghan bay into an actual town — including the narrow-gauge rail line hauling firewood into the forest that is now, without irony, marketed to tourists as the End of the World Train. The prison closed in 1947. Its former inmates, in a sense, are still the ones who built the city everyone comes to photograph.

Ninety percent of a very cold continent

Ushuaia's other identity — the one that has come to dominate the harbor — is as the departure point for Antarctica. Roughly nine in every ten Antarctic tourist voyages now leave from this single pier, a function of simple geography: the Antarctic Peninsula sits barely 600 miles across the Drake Passage, closer to Ushuaia than to any other inhabited place on Earth. What was a curiosity a generation ago has become an industry measured in the tens of thousands of passengers a season, and on a summer morning the waterfront can host half a dozen ships loading for the crossing at once, their hulls dwarfing the wooden buildings behind them.

The two identities sit uneasily side by side without quite touching. Tourists photograph the prison in the morning and board an icebreaker in the afternoon, and the city's whole economy has learned to run on both timelines — the slow one of a town that took a century to become permanent, and the fast one of a cruise season that now measures growth year over year.

Tourists photograph the prison in the morning and board an icebreaker in the afternoon.

Wind, water, and the end of a highway

South of town, Tierra del Fuego National Park runs the coastline down to Bahía Lapataia, where a modest wooden sign marks the official southern terminus of the Pan-American Highway — a road that, on paper, connects this bay to Prudhoe Bay, Alaska, roughly seventeen thousand kilometers north. Whether or not anyone has ever driven the whole thing continuously is a matter of some dispute, but the sign doesn't care; it simply marks where the road, and the continent, stop.

What the road leaves out is the water. The Beagle Channel does the work here that highways do elsewhere — it's how Estancia Harberton, the oldest ranch in Tierra del Fuego, gets its supplies, and it's how visitors reach Isla Martillo's penguin colonies, since no bridge or road serves either place. Lake Fagnano, an hour and a half north over the only mountain pass in the Fuegian Andes, drains toward Chile instead of the Atlantic, a small reminder that the border running through this island was drawn by treaty, not by the land itself.

A town that outgrew its reason for existing

Nothing about Ushuaia's founding logic — a flag, a prison, a claim against a rival government — explains why anyone would choose to live here now. And yet the population has grown past 80,000, most of it arrived in the last two generations, drawn by tax incentives, a growing tourism economy and, for some, simply the fact of living somewhere genuinely difficult to get to. The mountains that ring the town on three sides and the channel that closes the fourth make Ushuaia feel less like a city that expanded outward and more like one that filled in a space it was handed. It is still, more than a century after the first convict labor gang laid its first road, a town organized entirely around getting somewhere else — the park, the channel, the ice beyond it — and only incidentally around itself.
